card.title: Speech Writing — salutation, hooks, persuasive devices

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: **What it is:** writing meant to be SPOKEN — short sentences, rhythm, direct address. The examiner checks 'speakability'.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Trick 1: Speech frame: greeting → attention hook (question/quote/statistic) → three points with signposting ('firstly... secondly...') → memorable close (call to action).
Trick 2: Write for the EAR: short sentences, direct address ('my friends'), rhetorical questions — spoken rhythm is the style mark.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Test:** read your draft aloud — where you gasp, rewrite. Repeat your core phrase 2–3 times.  ·  **Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Q. Prepare a 2-minute speech on the importance of voting. (4 marks) — greeting, hook, two arguments, call to action.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: **Structure:** Salutation in order of seniority ('Respected Chairperson, judges, teachers, and my dear friends —') → Self-intro (if required) → Hook (question/fact/quotation) → 2–3 clear points ('First… Second… Finally…') → Persuasive devices (triads, repetition, rhetorical questions) → Strong closing appeal + 'Thank you.'  ·  **Grammar for the ear:** imperatives command action ('Let us pledge…'); rhetorical questions make the audience answer mentally; triads create rhythm.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 3: Time yourself: a 3-minute speech ≈ 350–400 words — over-length speeches lose the discipline mark.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q. How should a speech begin? (1 mark) — with a greeting and an attention-grabbing hook.
